explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD, the God of Israel, says, “Take from My hand this cup of the wine of wrath…” (Jeremiah 25:15). It comes straight from His hand into Jeremiah's. This is not a cup you pass around at a party, and I'd say the prophet knew it.

Close, friend, but that belt is from a different message. Jeremiah buys a linen belt and hides it in a rock, and it ends up ruined (Jeremiah 13:1-7). Here the LORD hands him a cup, and it's “the cup of the wine of wrath” (Jeremiah 25:15). Two different objects, two different messages.

That one is in Jeremiah, but it's in another spot. Jeremiah sees an almond branch in a vision at the very start of his book (Jeremiah 1:11). In this passage the LORD hands him “this cup of the wine of wrath” (Jeremiah 25:15). I mixed up my cutters on my first day too, so no shame.
That's it, baker. The LORD tells Jeremiah to “make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it” (Jeremiah 25:15). That's a big guest list. I'd have asked for a smaller one.

Priests are a good guess, but the text doesn't say that. The LORD says to make “all the nations to whom I send you drink from it” (Jeremiah 25:15). The list later in the passage is long, and it's kings and nations all the way down (Jeremiah 25:18-26).

Jeremiah is a prophet himself, so I see why this one tempts you. But the LORD says “all the nations to whom I send you” (Jeremiah 25:15). Jeremiah is the one carrying the cup, not the one in the lineup of drinkers.

Close, but no, friend. The LORD doesn't say famine here. He says they will drink “and stagger and go out of their minds, because of the sword that I will send among them” (Jeremiah 25:16). It's a sword, not a famine.

Right, friend. The word isn't famine, it's the sword. The LORD says they “will drink and stagger and go out of their minds, because of the sword that I will send among them” (Jeremiah 25:16). Paying attention to one little word like that is how a baker gets sharp.

That's right, baker. Jeremiah says, “So I took the cup from the LORD's hand…” (Jeremiah 25:17). No arguing, no stalling, no hopping backward on a gold base. He takes it, and I can only guess how heavy it felt.

I get why you'd think so, since it's a scary cup. But Jeremiah says, “So I took the cup from the LORD's hand…” (Jeremiah 25:17). He takes it. I think that took some real courage, because I would not have been that steady.

Yes, friend. If they refuse, Jeremiah is to say that the LORD of Hosts says, “You most certainly must drink it!” (Jeremiah 25:28). There's no opting out of this one. Saying no doesn't make the cup go away.

No passing, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, “You most certainly must drink it!” (Jeremiah 25:28). Nobody gets to hand it down the line like a hot tray out of the oven. The cup stays with whoever it was sent to.

There's no waiting list on this one. If a nation refuses, the LORD of Hosts says, “You most certainly must drink it!” (Jeremiah 25:28). The text gives them no extra time. Refusing doesn't change what's coming.

explanations.answer: The city that bears His Name
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears My Name…” (Jeremiah 25:29). This message already named Jerusalem at the head of the list (Jeremiah 25:18). Then He asks, “…how could you possibly go unpunished?”

Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, is a famous city, so I see the pull. But it's not named here. The LORD says the disaster begins with “the city that bears My Name” (Jeremiah 25:29). The list in this passage starts with Jerusalem and the cities of Judah (Jeremiah 25:18).

Damascus is a well-known city, but it's not what this verse says. The LORD says, “I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears My Name…” (Jeremiah 25:29). Damascus isn't in the list of this passage at all. Keep your eyes on the words in the text, friend.

explanations.answer: All the inhabitants of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, “…I am calling down a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth…” (Jeremiah 25:29). He starts with the city that bears His Name, and the sword is for everyone on earth. Nobody gets skipped.

explanations.answer: All the beasts of the field
explanations.explanation: Not the beasts, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, “…I am calling down a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth…” (Jeremiah 25:29). The words are about the inhabitants of the earth. The animals aren't in that verse.

explanations.answer: All the idols of the nations
explanations.explanation: The idols aren't named in this verse, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, “…I am calling down a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth…” (Jeremiah 25:29). It's the people who live on the earth. The sword comes down on them.

Yes, friend. Jeremiah is to say, “The LORD will roar from on high…” (Jeremiah 25:30). Then it says He will “roar loudly over His pasture.” That's a LOUD one, and my mustache is standing straight up just reading it.

I wish it were a whisper, friend, but no. The text says, “The LORD will roar from on high…” (Jeremiah 25:30). He will raise His voice from His holy habitation. That's about as far from a whisper as you can get.

Not a song this time, friend. Jeremiah is to say, “The LORD will roar from on high; He will raise His voice from His holy habitation…” (Jeremiah 25:30). This is a roar. I'd say it's not a tune you'd hum in the kitchen.

explanations.answer: The LORD brings a charge against the nations
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The verse says, “The tumult will resound to the ends of the earth because the LORD brings a charge against the nations.” (Jeremiah 25:31). That's a courtroom word, and the text says He brings judgment on all mankind. The sound goes out to the ends of the earth.

explanations.answer: The LORD shakes the mountains of the earth
explanations.explanation: Mountains shaking is a big image, but it's not what this verse says. The tumult resounds “because the LORD brings a charge against the nations” (Jeremiah 25:31). The reason is the charge He brings. Mountains aren't in the verse.

explanations.answer: The LORD opens the floodgates of the sky
explanations.explanation: Floodgates are from the story of Noah (Genesis 7:11), so it's a good memory. But here the reason is stated plainly: “…because the LORD brings a charge against the nations” (Jeremiah 25:31). No flood in this verse. It's the charge that makes the tumult.

Hard one, friend, and I think it hurts to read. The text says the opposite: “They will not be mourned, gathered, or buried.” (Jeremiah 25:33). They'll be spread from one end of the earth to the other. It's a heavy verse, so let's let it be heavy.
Right, baker. This is a heavy verse. It says those slain by the LORD on that day “will not be mourned, gathered, or buried.” (Jeremiah 25:33). I think it's one to read slowly.

Yes, friend. The text says, “Wail, you shepherds, and cry out; roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock.” (Jeremiah 25:34). The shepherds here are the leaders of the flock. The days of their slaughter have come.

No fighting in this verse, friend. The shepherds are told, “Wail, you shepherds, and cry out; roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock.” (Jeremiah 25:34). Next verse says that flight will evade them and escape will elude them (Jeremiah 25:35). Wailing is the order of the day.

I wish the news were happier, friend, but no. The shepherds are told, “Wail, you shepherds, and cry out; roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock.” (Jeremiah 25:34). The days of their slaughter have come. There's no singing in this verse.

That's right, baker. The text says, “Flight will evade the shepherds, and escape will elude the leaders of the flock.” (Jeremiah 25:35). I'd say no hiding spot is big enough, not even the back of a junk drawer. Believe me, I checked a few in my day.

I see why you'd hope for a way out, friend. But the text says, “Flight will evade the shepherds, and escape will elude the leaders of the flock.” (Jeremiah 25:35). They won't get away. It's a hard verse, and it says what it says.

Yes, friend. The text says, “…the LORD is destroying their pasture.” (Jeremiah 25:36). The shepherds lead the flock, so the pasture is their place. Then the next verse says the peaceful meadows have been silenced (Jeremiah 25:37).

Good thinking, but the temple isn't in these verses. The text says, “…the LORD is destroying their pasture.” (Jeremiah 25:36). Shepherds go with pasture, and that's the word it uses. Hold onto it, baker.

The harvest is a fair guess, since it's about the land. But the verse says, “…the LORD is destroying their pasture.” (Jeremiah 25:36). The shepherds are the ones wailing, so a pasture fits. The word harvest isn't in the verse.

That's right, baker. The text says, “…their land has been made a desolation by the sword of the oppressor, and because of the fierce anger of the LORD.” (Jeremiah 25:38). Both are in the same line. A sword was in the message from the very beginning, back at the cup (Jeremiah 25:16).

Famine is a good guess, but it's not in this line. The text says the land has been made a desolation “by the sword of the oppressor, and because of the fierce anger of the LORD.” (Jeremiah 25:38). It's the sword. The word famine doesn't show up in this passage.

Locusts are in the Bible, friend, but they aren't in this line. The land has been made a desolation “by the sword of the oppressor, and because of the fierce anger of the LORD.” (Jeremiah 25:38). It's a sword that ends the passage. Locusts never come up in these verses.
